title: Anchoring Enterprise GenAI with Knowledge Graphs: Jonathan Lowe (Pfizer), Stephen Chin (Neo4j)

primary.label: Retrieval, Search & Knowledge
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on GraphRAG, combining vector search with knowledge graph traversal for enterprise retrieval and explainability. Pfizer's biopharma manufacturing maps to healthcare life sciences, enterprise workflows to enterprise operations, and knowledge graphs to search and knowledge. Pfizer is described as an early production adopter with a deployed GraphRAG system. Requires familiarity with RAG and knowledge graphs but remains accessible to practitioners. Recorded conference session from AI Engineer Summit 2025 Leadership Track. All evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript.

summary: Stephen Chin and Jonathan Lowe address the high failure rate of enterprise GenAI projects, citing Gartner's prediction that 30% will be abandoned by end of 2025. The primary failure mode is lacking a viable, monetizable business use case. Jonathan presents his work at Pfizer on technology transfer—scaling biopharma manufacturing from lab bench to industrial scale (millions of doses per day), which traditionally takes years due to sifting through hundreds of thousands of documents. Manufacturing worker average tenure dropped from 20 years (2019) to 3 years, making knowledge capture urgent as boomer expertise retires. Their solution loads millions of documents into a knowledge graph with hierarchically structured chunks (document, block, paragraph, line) for optimized similarity search. Jonathan then details stakeholder navigation in a 100,000+ person company: executives set aspirational taglines, chief officers translate to domain goals, mid-level managers demand concrete cost savings and revenue metrics, and additional obstacles include conflicting client partners, vendor build-vs-buy pressures, and colleague resistance. He recommends starting with end users and tailoring messaging upward. The session transitions to technology: Jonathan chose graph databases because Pfizer's data involved genealogic sequences, recipes, social networks, hierarchies, and time series—all natural graph applications. Beyond traversal performance, team productivity improved dramatically—data consolidation tasks that took 3 months now take 3 weeks or less. Stephen explains the GraphRAG spectrum: direct LLM usage lacks enterprise context; baseline vector RAG pulls organizational knowledge but yields generic answers with hallucinations; GraphRAG combines vector search with knowledge graph traversal for precise, contextually rich results. GraphRAG also enables better governance through access controls on graph nodes and superior explainability, since answers reference concrete graphs, nodes, and edges rather than statistical probabilities in vector space. Microsoft wrote the seminal GraphRAG paper, and Pfizer is an early production adopter.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: GenAI Project Failures and Business Case Introduction
sections.summary: Stephen Chin opens by citing Gartner's prediction that 30% of GenAI projects will be abandoned by end of 2025. Audience polls confirm most have not yet reached production. The biggest failure mode is identified as lacking a real, monetizable business use case. Jonathan Lowe is introduced as someone who has successfully navigated organizational challenges to build a production GenAI system at Pfizer.

sections.title: Pfizer Technology Transfer Use Case
sections.summary: Jonathan explains technology transfer in biopharma—scaling from lab bench to industrial production (millions of doses/day), which takes years due to sifting through hundreds of thousands of documents. Manufacturing worker tenure dropped from 20 years (2019) to 3 years, making knowledge capture urgent. The solution loads millions of documents into a knowledge graph with hierarchically structured chunks (document, block, paragraph, line) to optimize similarity search and iteratively improve chunking.

sections.title: Organizational Navigation in Large Companies
sections.summary: Jonathan details stakeholder navigation in a 100,000+ person company. He describes a layered approach: executives set aspirational taglines, chief officers translate to domain goals, level 2-3 managers demand concrete cost/efficiency numbers, client partners may conflict on scope, vendors push build-vs-buy, and colleagues may create friendly fire. He recommends starting with end users who want tools removing tedious work while delivering accurate, performant results.

sections.title: GraphRAG Architecture and Benefits
sections.summary: Jonathan explains why graph databases were chosen at Pfizer: genealogic sequences, recipes, social networks, hierarchies, and time series were prevalent data patterns. Beyond traversal performance, team productivity improved—data consolidation from 3 months to 3 weeks. Stephen outlines the GraphRAG spectrum: direct LLM (lacks context), baseline vector RAG (generic, hallucinations), and GraphRAG (precise, governed, explainable). GraphRAG combines vector search with knowledge graph traversal, enabling access controls on graph nodes and explainability via concrete nodes and edges rather than statistical probabilities. Microsoft wrote the seminal GraphRAG paper; Pfizer is an early production adopter.
